summary: Refunded tickets still admit at an OFFLINE gate — revocation does not reach scanners
description:
Found by the TKT-157 adversarial review (finding F1, accepted as a real gap and rejected as a change to that ticket).

TKT-157 refuses a refunded ticket at a **live** gate. An **offline** scanner has no way to learn a ticket was refunded, so it admits the holder, and `ReconcileAdmission` then faithfully records that admission — `entry`/`redeemed`/`duplicate_admit` appended after the refund, with a chain that verifies clean and proves a refunded ticket was used.

**Blocking reconciliation is the wrong fix and was rejected on those grounds.** The person is already inside; refusing to record it would falsify the trail rather than protect a gate (ADR-038 §4). The missing capability is **revocation propagation to scanners** — a scanner/offline-distribution feature in ADR-025's territory.

Also considered and rejected for TKT-157: raising an integrity alarm on reconciling a refunded ticket. `oweAlarm` writes to the **integrity** alarm channel, which means *the chain is suspect*; a refunded-but-admitted ticket is not an integrity event, and TKT-147 is already open to replace that channel's free-text reason with fixed reason codes. Overloading it now would make TKT-147 worse.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- [ ] A scanner that went offline before a refund, and syncs after it, does not admit the refunded holder — or, if it already did, the operator is told through a channel that means *this* rather than *the chain is suspect*.
- [ ] Whatever the mechanism, reconciliation still records what physically happened. An occurrence is never dropped to make the trail look better.
- [ ] The revocation feed is bounded and testable offline (no live-network assumption at a gate).

Quality gates: `make check` green; `access verify-lifecycle` green; contract tests.

binding.rule: Money is integer minor units + ISO currency code — floats are banned on money paths.

Traceability is a must, for money and tickets: money-relevant records land as immutable, hash-chained, signed journal entries from the first order (corrections = compensating entries; read models = projections), and every ticket/entitlement state change (issued, delivered, transferred, resold, exchanged, redeemed, reissued, invalidated) is an append-only lifecycle event linked to its order.

governingAdrs.why: Every lifecycle event goes through store.appendLifecycle — the verifier asserts one-to-one coverage, so a direct INSERT into lifecycle_events reads as tampering and fails `access verify-lifecycle` in the gate. Canonical forms are pinned by golden literals; changing a byte is a canonical-version migration, not a test update. Also: name the adversary before writing 'tamper-evident'.

Inventory's claim transaction is the contention path. Giving capacity back must go through the same row-locked transaction discipline; a plain UPDATE outside it can drive confirmed_quantity negative or double-return under concurrency.
Capacity adjustments clamp rather than reject. Returning capacity must not let availability exceed the pool's capacity, and the clamp reasoning is the precedent for what to do when it would.

Corrections are COMPENSATING ENTRIES, never mutations. A refund/exchange appends a new signed fact; the original sale fact and its hash link are untouched. The payments journal has a DB trigger that raises on UPDATE/DELETE — any design that 'adjusts' a fact is rejected by the database, not by review.

If any domain event payload changes or a new one is published: bump on CONSUMER SEMANTICS, not parse compatibility, and consumers dispatch on `schema` BEFORE decoding `data`. A fixture built from the type under test cannot fail.

Fail closed. Responses are validated against the spec; an undeclared status code becomes a 500. Every new endpoint must declare every status it can answer, and a downstream answer commerce cannot validate aborts rather than degrades.

Contract-first. A new operation is written in the service's openapi.yaml first, then `openapi_gen.go` / `api-types.gen.ts` are regenerated and COMMITTED before the gate runs — check-generate diffs against HEAD, so an uncommitted regen reads as drift.
Commerce and inventory ARE inside the smoke happy-path coverage gate. A new documented 2xx operation must be exercised through the running stack or the suite fails.

Migrations run out-of-band via each binary's `migrate` subcommand as a one-shot Compose job. Add the SQL under the service's internal/store/migrations/ with the next number; the server path never migrates.

objective.note: A refunded ticket that still opens an offline gate is a real revenue and access-control hole; TKT-157 closed only the live half and said so.

scope.note: The mechanism is undecided: revocation list pushed to scanners, short-TTL credentials, or an online check with an offline grace. Each has different offline-tolerance costs.

uncertainties.note: How long an offline scanner may lag, and what it is allowed to do while lagging, is a product decision — not an engineering one.

dependencies.note: Belongs with TKT-19 (access control & scanning) and interacts with ADR-025's offline reconciliation contract.

approach.note: Blocked on the scope decision above.

first_slice.note: Blocked on the scope decision above.

success.note: Blocked on the scope decision above.

context_memo.note: Inherited from TKT-157; ADR-038 §4 states the bound this ticket lifts.

comments.body:
<!-- sdlc:stage=backlog kind=readiness -->
### ❌ Implementation readiness — FAIL (deliberately)

Not a defect: the mechanism is a product decision nobody has taken. Shaping starts with *how long may an offline scanner lag, and what may it do while lagging* — not with a plan. The board will refuse Gate 1 until that is answered, which is correct.
